title: “Chaconne and Triple Fugue”: Nods to Tradition in Prelude and Fugue No.13, Book II
content_blocks: I come to the final post about the individual Preludes and Fugues with the last of the second set, the Chaconne and Triple Fugue. Completing the trend of fewer and fewer preparations inside the piano as Book II progresses, there are no preparations used in this celebration of unaltered piano sound. At the same time, this concludes the trajectory of questioning the idea of solo piano begun with the whistling in No.1, followed by the singing in No.12, and the optional second piano part at the end of No.12: this pair of pieces is for two pianos.

It also finishes off an overall trend of progressing from new, “synthetic” modes used in the first book returning slowly to recognizable modes from the end of Book I through Book II: we start Prelude No.13 in a very recognizable, essentially completely diatonic (that is, without any altered notes) C minor. But there are two underlying goals in all of these pieces that guarantee that such a simple tonal world cannot be taken for granted: questioning (or, as I put it in “Exploding the Notion of ‘Preludes and Fugues in Various Keys’, June 23, 2025 “exploding”) everything, and encouraging us all not to be afraid of the new. So onto this simple, diatonic C minor I overlay a steadily increasing chromaticism, to the point where tonality is obscured (although not obliterated) by the chromatic ooze.

A traditional chaconne employs a simple, repeated bass-line and chord progression usually four or eight bars long.  Here the first statement of the chaconne is only one measure long, but each time it repeats it grows by a measure; the final statement is 18 measures long.  By the end of the prelude, too, there are at least seven (at times eight) simultaneous different lines.

This leads into the fugue, which retains only the barest shadow of tonality.  This five-voice fugue—growing at one point to a total of seven voices—boasts at least three countersubjects, plus two additional fugue subjects which are introduced over the course of the piece (one of these additional fugue subjects is in a 25/16 meter, contrasting and conflicting dramatically with the main 3/4 meter).  By the end of the piece, these are combined into a triple fugue, to round out the entire two books of preludes and fugues.

The prelude and fugue, as the “last hurrah” of both this set of pieces and of the two books of preludes and fugues, expresses this position both through its excesses (of figuration and chromaticism, most especially in the Chaconne, and also in the very nature of a five-voice triple fugue), but also in the way that the fugue subject refers back to the theme of Fugue No.2, Bells.  In that fugue the actual pitch content of the notes played is obscured by the preparations; here, without any preparations, the pitch content emerges clearly.

These pieces were inspired by Russian-American artist Naum Gabo’s Linear Construction No.1 and Linear Construction No.2, in the way that a seemingly-simple and familiar shape can grow and morph and become something complicated, rich, and new.

Steve and Michael, who shared a piano teacher and once played a piano duo as kids, reunite for this fabulous performance. The fluency with which they play this overlapping lines—some heavily chromatic, some diatonic, many of them packing zillions of notes into very short time-spans—never ceases to amaze me. You can see it for yourself in this combined video! And with that pull-out-all-the-stops performance of this dense piece of music, the two volumes of preludes and fugues—and my blog posts about those individual pieces—comes to an end. I hope to continue blogging into the future, although I don’t know just what I’ll write about. Come back and pay a visit to see!
